paragraphs: Before studying abroad, I had no overseas experience other than going once to Taiwan on a school trip, and I did not really know what lay outside Japan. In addition, having lived 23 years surrounded by Japanese, I did not really know what it feels like to be surrounded by another language around the clock, and I wanted to find out. To be honest, it was not that I particularly wanted to go because I was interested in foreign medicine; I simply applied out of curiosity, in a light-hearted way. Even so, last February I studied properly every day and got an English score, in July I took an English interview, and my study abroad in Germany was decided. After that I crammed in a bit of medical English here and there and set off for Germany.

The first shock, when I arrived at Frankfurt Airport, was that I struggled even to buy a single piece of bread. Between the unfriendly clerk, unlike in Japan, and me speaking halting English, even buying just a cream bun was extremely difficult. (The toilet bowls were also tall, made for Germans.) After that I headed to my lodging, where I was to receive a thorough baptism of Germany. The owner lived in the lodging together with the guests. At first, when I greeted him and we talked cheerfully, I thought, what a cheerful and kind person. However, since I had been told beforehand that the rent was "around 700 euros," when I asked "so it is around 700 euros?", he said "It is 800, though?", the atmosphere suddenly changed, and I was baffled. The message app history certainly said about 700, so is this a deviation that fits within "around"? When I thought so, he began going on about how prices had risen after the war in Ukraine and so on. It was there that I first realised I should stop trusting this adult too much. This landlord was extremely hysterical about money and the cleanliness of the house, and I met for the first time a person who panics and with whom conversation breaks down.

School life began with going to forensic medicine, and while seeing various cases here and there, February passed gently. Then it became March and I was to rotate through neurosurgery, where I met one student. She was a third-year student from another university and, as an internship during her vacation, was to rotate through neurosurgery for one month as well. At first I was taken aback. I had never thought that I would suddenly spend the whole day with a student from another university, the two of us in the clerkship. But as we spent time together, her character became apparent. The first thing I noticed was that her NO and YES were incredibly clear. One of the doctors was a person who constantly offered us coffee, and I somehow could not refuse even a second cup and drank it, but she often declined with NO, and even when the doctor asked persistently "Really, you don't want any?", she kept saying NO. At first I thought she had guts, but gradually I realised that, conversely, whatever she said YES to was an absolute YES. I realised that because that is so clear, there is no need to be considerate in developing a relationship, and it is very easy to be with her. It means the possibility that she is doing something reluctantly is extremely low. That was fresh to me to begin with. Being taught how to eat a pretzel and gnawing on apples together while waiting were, in their own way, somehow interesting days. In neurosurgery it was mainly observation, and I could not scrub in on operations.

Here let me note one difference between German and Japanese medical students. It is without doubt that education is given about two years earlier than for Japanese students, as I felt it. I felt this from talking with her. She did blood draws on patients smoothly, and she had medical knowledge so extensive I could hardly believe she was a third-year, and I was often taken aback in discussion classes. Apparently, since there are no liberal arts subjects (?), medical education can start early, but my pride was torn up nicely and I felt I had to study. I also thought it was contradictory in the first place that she was supposed to be on a month of vacation yet was doing a one-month internship. But I thought that this is how they experience the clinical setting from early on. In the last week, the three of us, a doctor from Chile, she and I, had a farewell party. Somehow it turned out that we ate Vietnamese food and shared things like edamame, and when splitting the bill she paid first and I paid last, and of course I had intended to pay for the edamame, but she had already paid for it, and I thought in my heart, ah, she beat me to it. Edamame for 5 euros.

And by dealing with various doctors here, I noticed something. It was that among the doctors there were people who completely ignored me. I think this is something one can hardly experience in Japan. Thinking about it properly, there is indeed no short-term benefit in being nice to a student who comes from outside and stays only a month. In a sense it was natural. I cannot remember how many times I said hello and they did not even meet my eyes and ignored me. Each time my heart was worn down. And there was one more thing, an experience that could even be called a setback, in this study abroad. It happened in the next department, neuroradiology, which I had chosen myself beforehand. There was a reason: after a month of only observing in neurosurgery, I wanted to use my hands. I had heard from a senior who studied at the same university five years ago that he was allowed to do a lot of catheter work, and I thought, I am also interested in the brain, so let me change and do procedures. However, no matter how much time passed, the doctors never asked whether I would like to try, and I stood there watching with my nerves on edge. But three days before the end, I really wanted to do something, and I dared to ask a doctor to please let me assist with anything. Then the doctor's mood and expression changed, and he said, "You are an exchange student, so you cannot take responsibility, so it is better to just stand and watch." This was a shock so big to me that I truly cannot put it into words. At Nagoya University in Japan I could often get into the operative field without having to plead, and I had not imagined that it would be such a distant and long road here. Then I learned one thing. That the heartache of being refused is something one has to get used to to some extent, and that if one still wants to do it, one has no choice but to keep knocking on the wall.

From there I went on to do a clerkship in otorhinolaryngology. There too I was refused by one doctor. That person allowed other German students to scrub in with him, yet only I could not. Even so, I kept constantly asserting that I wanted to scrub in, and I was finally able to assist another doctor with a cochlear implant operation. It was the first time I scrubbed up and assisted in Germany. At that time I was truly close to tears, and the sense of achievement after it was over was tremendous. The joy of having been able to contribute to German medicine. As an aside, there I apparently gained the trust of a nurse in a managerial position (?), and we became friendly. When there was another chance to ask the male doctor I mentioned earlier about an operation, I was again told, as if it were natural, something like "You should just stand there," but then that nurse made a second request on my behalf. Then the doctor's attitude changed completely, and it became something like "Come on in," and I went into the operation with that person. After it was over I went to that nurse and said thank you. She asked, "Did you learn something?", and I answered that I learned a lot. I felt anew that trusting relationships in the workplace are important.

Also, through the nurses and the daily examinations, I learned a little German by ear. Each time someone around me taught me new German, it was only sound and I did not know the spelling well, so it was close to the natural language acquisition of a baby, and the nurses patiently taught me German with gestures like a baby, and I realised that this is how my mother and the people around me patiently taught me Japanese.

I have written about various things I felt, but what I feel I grew most is that I no longer get hurt and depressed by small things. Through the experiences described above, I feel that I have become stronger. And above all, what I felt most was the importance of perseverance. I never gave up going to the clerkship until the end, and even in hard times I clearly told the people around me what I wanted to do, and I think I became able to widen my possibilities. As a result, not only in terms of study but also by making friends, it was overall a good study abroad. I can only be grateful to my parents, my friends and my teachers.
